article_title: The Illusion of Competence: Self-Perceived Digital Literacy and AI Readiness Among European Secondary Students
citation: Nicolas Rodriguez-Alvarez, Alan Martin Blanch-Marsolini, Samuel Vara-Gutierrez, Hugo Gil-Garcia, Javier Calzon-Dueñas, and Fernando Rodriguez-Merino. (2026). The Illusion of Competence: Self-Perceived Digital Literacy and AI Readiness Among European Secondary Students. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26010
title: Open CC-BY 4.0 dataset of digital self-efficacy responses (N=243) on Zenodo
description: The study's fully anonymized dataset (n=243) has been released into the public domain under a CC-BY 4.0 license. According to the article, "The dataset, encompassing all demographic variables and Likert-scale responses, along with its comprehensive codebook, is freely accessible via the Zenodo repository", supporting reproducibility of the self-efficacy analyses.
requirements: Comprehensive codebook accompanies the data for reuse
constraints: Data come from a convenience sample of three institutions in Spain and Ireland
target_learning_goals: self-perceived digital literacy and AI readiness measurement
key_sources: Nicolas Rodriguez-Alvarez, Alan Martin Blanch-Marsolini, Samuel Vara-Gutierrez, Hugo Gil-Garcia, Javier Calzon-Dueñas, and Fernando Rodriguez-Merino. (2026). The Illusion of Competence: Self-Perceived Digital Literacy and AI Readiness Among European Secondary Students. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26010

article_title: Behavioral clustering for adaptive learning object recommendation in higher education using learning analytics for personalized student success
citation: Najem, K., Zaoui Seghroucheni, Y., & Ziti, S. (2026). Behavioral clustering for adaptive learning object recommendation in higher education using learning analytics for personalized student success. Discover Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44217-026-02181-7
title: Student Performance and Learning Behavior Dataset for Educational Analytics (Zenodo, N = 14,003)
description: A publicly accessible dataset of anonymized student records deposited on Zenodo, described by the article as "a publicly available dataset of 14,003 anonymized student records" with 16 attributes covering behavior, engagement, psychological attributes, demographics, and academic outcomes. It was compiled by merging two publicly available Kaggle datasets into merged_dataset.csv, with a Jupyter Notebook (Project.ipynb) deposited alongside. Twelve features served as clustering inputs; demographics and performance outcomes were reserved for validation.
requirements: Open-access deposition on Zenodo under CC0 with no personally identifiable information, supporting reproducibility and follow-up research
constraints: The source materials do not document the original institution type(s), source population, data-collection period, or instrument; the dataset is not a live LMS log stream
target_learning_goals: behavioral profiling for adaptive learning object recommendation
examples: The study's clustering, ANOVA, Tukey HSD, and chi-square analyses were all performed on this dataset
key_sources: Najem, K., Zaoui Seghroucheni, Y., & Ziti, S. (2026). Behavioral clustering for adaptive learning object recommendation in higher education using learning analytics for personalized student success. Discover Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44217-026-02181-7

article_title: Teacher Self-Efficacy and Its Effects on Classroom Processes, Student Academic Adjustment, and Teacher Well-Being
citation: M. Zee, H.M.Y. Koomen. (2016). Teacher self-efficacy and its effects on classroom processes, student academic adjustment, and teacher well-being: A synthesis of 40 years of research. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315626801
title: Criteria-based review corpus of 165 teacher self-efficacy articles
description: The evidence base for this synthesis is a corpus of 165 eligible articles on teacher self-efficacy, selected through a "criteria-based review approach". The corpus spans 40 years of TSE research and underpins the review's conclusions about links between TSE and classroom processes, students' academic adjustment, and teachers' psychological well-being, including the burnout findings and the small set of indirect-effect studies.
requirements: Articles had to meet the review's inclusion criteria to be counted as eligible for analysis
target_learning_goals: teacher self-efficacy and its consequences for classroom processes, student adjustment, and teacher well-being
examples: 165 eligible articles included for analysis via a criteria-based review approach
key_sources: M. Zee, H.M.Y. Koomen. (2016). Teacher self-efficacy and its effects on classroom processes, student academic adjustment, and teacher well-being: A synthesis of 40 years of research. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315626801

article_title: A Systematic Review of Self-Regulated Learning through Integration of Multimodal Data and Artificial Intelligence
citation: Susanne de Mooij, Joni Lämsä, Lyn Lim, Olli Aksela, Shruti Athavale, Inti Bistolfi, Flora Jin, Tongguang Li, Roger Azevedo, Maria Bannert, Dragan Gašević, Sanna Järvelä, Inge Molenaar. (2025). A Systematic Review of Self-Regulated Learning through Integration of Multimodal Data and Artificial Intelligence. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10028-0
title: Open-source database of SRL constructs and multimodal indicators
description: To address variation in operational definitions of CAMM processes when applying multimodal data and analytics, the review's authors provide an open-source database hosted on Zenodo (https://zenodo.org/records/15481052). The article states "This database can be utilized to gain more detailed information about the SRL constructs within each CAMM process and the related indicators derived from multimodal data and analytics." It supports researchers in comparing how constructs and indicators were operationalised across the 142 included studies.
requirements: Researchers seeking construct-level detail on CAMM operationalisations across the included studies
target_learners: SRL researchers and learning analytics practitioners
target_learning_goals: valid and reliable measurement of CAMM processes underlying self-regulated learning
examples: The database accompanies the review's mapping of studies onto the SMA grid and its coding of CAMM processes, data streams, and analytical methods
key_sources: Susanne de Mooij, Joni Lämsä, Lyn Lim, Olli Aksela, Shruti Athavale, Inti Bistolfi, Flora Jin, Tongguang Li, Roger Azevedo, Maria Bannert, Dragan Gašević, Sanna Järvelä, Inge Molenaar. article_title: Native learning ability and not age determines the effects of brain stimulation
citation: Maceira-Elvira, P., Popa, T., Schmid, A.-C., Cadic-Melchior, A., Müller, H., & Schaer, R. (2024). Native learning ability and not age determines the effect of brain stimulation on motor skill acquisition. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00278-y

examples: The repository contains the likelihoods estimated for each individual, referenced from Fig. 1

article_title: Applying Large Language Models to Enhance Dialogue and Communication Analysis for Adaptive Team Training
citation: Spain, R., Min, W., Kumaran, V., Pande, V., Saville, J., & Lester, J. (2024). Applying Large Language Models to Enhance Dialogue and Communication Analysis for Adaptive Team Training. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-4565500/v1
title: Zero-shot LLMs refined through prompt engineering offer a promising means for supporting dialogue act recognition with minimal training data
description: The article concludes that zero-shot LLMs, refined through prompt engineering, offer a promising means for supporting dialogue act recognition, and that prompt refinements—particularly those addressing confusion between dialogue acts—can lead to superior recall rates for challenging labels. This principle supports incorporating these capabilities into future training systems to provide learners and instructors with tailored feedback to support and improve team communication behaviors. The article states this approach "paves the way for developing AI-enabled training systems that can adapt to the dynamic communication styles of different teams".
requirements: Access to a proprietary LLM such as GPT-4 or an open-source alternative such as T5
Iterative prompt refinement targeting label confusions identified through error analysis
constraints: T5 remains a viable option because it is open-source, whereas GPT-4 is proprietary; this distinction becomes more critical as implementation scales up in training settings with multiple sessions where the costs of model deployment are significant
In a training environment where T5 models have not been trained with data from that specific training, GPT-4 with zero-shot or few-shot learning might significantly outperform T5
target_learners: team members in military squad training exercises
instructors and researchers using adaptive team training systems
examples: The article reports that GPT-4 achieved 77.30% accuracy on the held-out test set without requiring fine-tuning with training data or extensive hyperparameter optimization
key_sources: Spain, R., Min, W., Kumaran, V., Pande, V., Saville, J., & Lester, J. (2024). Applying Large Language Models to Enhance Dialogue and Communication Analysis for Adaptive Team Training. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-4565500/v1

article_title: To Give Control to Learners or Not? A Comparative Study of Two Ways of Teaching Listening
citation: Yushan Wang. (2010). To Give Control to Learners or Not? A Comparative Study of Two Ways of Teaching Listening. English Language Teaching, Vol. 3, No. 2. http://www.ccsenet.org/elt
title: The zero class hour listening teaching model
description: A listening teaching model in which the teacher mainly gives learning aims, assignments and methods while students learn independently inside and outside the classroom and attend the final examination. The article identifies three ways of carrying it out (web courses, radio broadcasting, language labs) and chose language labs because students there have the greatest control. Students gain control over "the length of listening", pace, speed, way, place and material of listening, with the teacher checking results through questions, quizzes and tests.
requirements: A teacher still gives short lectures on listening skills and assigns compulsory and optional tasks
Digital devices or equipment allowing students to change delivery speed and choose materials
constraints: In the web-course and radio-broadcasting variants, students still have little control of pace, way, speed and material
target_learners: second-year non-English major university students in China
examples: In the study, the experimental group finished both compulsory and optional listening tasks outside class while the control group completed the compulsory part in class, both taught by the same teacher for two months
key_sources: Yushan Wang. (2010). To Give Control to Learners or Not? A Comparative Study of Two Ways of Teaching Listening. English Language Teaching, Vol. 3, No. 2. http://www.ccsenet.org/elt

article_title: A Case Study of a Co-Instructed Multidisciplinary Senior Capstone Project in Sustainability
citation: Rhee, J., Oyamot, C., Parent, D., Speer, L., Basu, A., & Gerston, L. (2014). A Case Study of a Co-instructed Multidisciplinary Senior Capstone Project in Sustainability. Advances in Engineering Education. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED
title: ZEM House zero-emissions demonstration house multidisciplinary capstone project
description: The ZEM House was "a 100-square-ft demonstration house that emits no greenhouse gases during operation," designed in fall 2010 by students from five disciplines and built and tested in spring 2011. Subprojects covered public policy, HVAC/structure, economic feasibility, user needs, and the photovoltaic energy system. The project generated campus contest placements, a conference presentation, gallery exhibition, and finalist status in the EDF Sustainable Design Challenge in Paris.
requirements: Disciplinary subprojects assigned across the five participating disciplines
Shared supervision and facilities across co-instructed courses
constraints: The 100-square-ft footprint was a self-imposed constraint to increase campus build-site options
target_learners: senior capstone students in engineering, industrial design, business, and political science
examples: Over $15K of donations were solicited from local companies, including solar photovoltaic panels, batteries, and lumber.
key_sources: Rhee, J., Oyamot, C., Parent, D., Speer, L., Basu, A., & Gerston, L. (2014). A Case Study of a Co-instructed Multidisciplinary Senior Capstone Project in Sustainability. Advances in Engineering Education. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1076079

article_title: Performance and reliability of large language models on the European Board of Hand Surgery examination: a multi-model evaluation study.
citation: Güler Ibrahim, Muir Lindsay, Grieb Gerrit, Moog Philipp, Kraus Armin, Stelling Henrik. (2026). Performance and reliability of large language models on the European Board of Hand Surgery examination: a multi-model evaluation study. The Journal of Hand Surgery, European Volume. https://doi.org/10.1177/17531934261436305
title: Standardized zero-shot CO-STAR-prompted multi-run web-interface evaluation protocol for assessing LLMs on high-stakes examinations.
description: The study employed a standardized zero-shot evaluation protocol in which all 10 LLMs completed five independent runs across all 300 examination statements through publicly available web interfaces rather than APIs, "reflecting the predominant interaction patterns of clinical and educational end users". The prompt followed the CO-STAR structure (Context, Objective, Style, Tone, Audience, Response format) to specify task parameters and required concise true/false answers without explanations or hedging. Session independence was maintained by starting each run in a new browser session or incognito window, clearing all previous chat history and creating a fresh conversation for every evaluation, with model order randomized across runs and timestamps and exact model versions documented for each session.
requirements: Identical zero-shot prompt across models and runs to assess pre-trained medical knowledge and minimize elicitation bias

Strict session-independence protocols: new browser session or incognito window per run, cleared chat history, fresh conversation per evaluation, randomized model order, documented timestamps and model versions
Double data entry performed independently by two researchers with quality control verification of response completeness and automated flagging of discrepancies
constraints: Evaluation through web interfaces may introduce small differences compared with API use but better reflects real-world access

Results represent a single time point and model behaviour may change with subsequent updates; provider-side updates can alter accuracy, calibration or response style without explicit disclosure, limiting longitudinal comparability
Sources of variability from interface behavior or transient model updates cannot be fully excluded
target_learners: Researchers evaluating LLM performance in medical education and assessment
Medical educators and examination bodies considering AI evaluation methodologies
target_learning_goals: Reproducible, fair comparison of LLM performance on high-stakes knowledge assessments
Reliable measurement of inter-run stability in AI evaluation studies
examples: The study followed CONSORT-AI reporting standards and adhered to current best practices for medical AI evaluation
key_sources: Güler Ibrahim, Muir Lindsay, Grieb Gerrit, Moog Philipp, Kraus Armin, Stelling Henrik. (2026). Performance and reliability of large language models on the European Board of Hand Surgery examination: a multi-model evaluation study. The Journal of Hand Surgery, European Volume. https://doi.org/10.1177/17531934261436305

article_title: Evaluation of MCQs from MOOCs for common item writing flaws.
citation: Costello E, Holland JC, Kirwan C. (2018). Evaluation of MCQs from MOOCs for common item writing flaws. BMC Research Notes. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13104-018-3959-4
title: Open Zenodo dataset of 204 MOOC MCQs with dual-evaluator flaw ratings
description: A spreadsheet dataset collated from MCQ items in 18 MOOCs in medical health education, life sciences and computer science. Two researchers "critically reviewed 204 questions using an evidence-based evaluation protocol" covering 15 specific item flaws, recording per-evaluator responses, combined consensus evaluations, programmatically computed quantitative item features, and summary flaw-prevalence statistics. The data "can be freely and openly accessed on Zenodo".
requirements: Quiz question text itself is not included because it is copyright of the MOOC platform providers; further aspects are shared on request
constraints: Sample is a convenience sample of English-language MOOCs in the researchers' areas of expertise, enrolling during the data collection window, not a true random sample
target_learners: MOOC designers and assessment researchers in higher education
target_learning_goals: Quality assurance of multiple-choice assessment items in online courses
examples: Each MCQ received a unique id of the format qi–j (quiz i, question j), and evaluators entered judgements such as whether the item contained plausible distractors via a pre-populated Google Form
key_sources: Costello E, Holland JC, Kirwan C. (2018). Evaluation of MCQs from MOOCs for common item writing flaws. BMC Research Notes. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13104-018-3959-4
